newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serbs fail to show at first assembly session.
newsitem.headline: Serbs fail to show at first assembly session.

text.p: Moslem and Croat legislators opened Bosnia's new inter-ethnic parliament on Saturday, ignoring a boycott by Serbs who refused to swear an oath to Bosnian statehood.
International mediators failed to broker a compromise that would satisfy hardline nationalist Momcilo Krajisnik, the Serb member of the newly-elected presidency, and Serb members of parliament.
After delaying the ceremony for several hours, Croat and Moslem deputies held the first session without the 10 Serb deputies and Krajisnik.
As foreign dignitaries looked on, Moslem and Croat politicians signed an oath of loyalty to the Bosnian constitution on the stage of Sarajevo's national theatre.

The oath was unacceptable to Krajisnik and the Bosnian Serbs elected to the parliament as it obliges members to swear loyalty to Bosnia as a unitary state, a concept which the Serbs have bitterly opposed.

The oath read in part: "I commit myself to support and defend the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina." It also calls for defending the equality of national communities and "to fully respect the peace agreement".

Carl Bildt, the international High Representative to Bosnia, said: "This ceremony was prepared in very close technical cooperation with (the Serbs) down to the last details like the music, the decorations, the seating arrangements and God knows what... They are playing games."
Croat and Moslem deputies decided that it was important to hold the session to establish postwar governing bodes for Bosnia and bolster the peace process.
"In view of the constitutional continuity of the country I thought it was very important to proceed," Bildt said.
Bildt's office, correcting an earlier account from one aide, said the ceremony carried legal weight as an inaugural session of parliament despite the Serb boycott.
"In our view this is the first session of the House of Representatives. It has full legitimacy...," Michael Maclay, a spokesman for Bildt, told Reuters.
The 42-member House of Representatives and the three-man collective presidency were chosen in general elections on September 14, nine months after the signing of the Dayton peace accord.
After the Moslem and Croat presidents signed the oath, Izetbegovic delivered what he said was his original speech which he had prepared assuming the Serbs would show up.
Addressing the absent Serb representatives, he said: "Feel safe, this is your town too, because Sarajevo is the capital of Bosnia-Herzegovina."
Two of the 10 Serb deputies who belong to an opposition party were willing to drive down to Sarajevo for the session but were apparently prevented from doing so by their own authorities.
